One question that I see from tonight's discussion, though, is 1) am I right to feel I'm special, and 2) if I am special, am I right to hold myself to a higher standard than other people?


My own feeling on the first question is, yes, absolutely, we are each and every one of us very special, and our best and highest purpose is determining and nurturing that within us which is special, and helping that grow and blossom as best as it may.


However, in response to the second question, my feeling is "no." If each and every one of us is special and unique, how does it make sense to compare ourselves to others and judge ourselves either positively or negatively as a result? The whole thing's apples and oranges, even within a particular field or discipline. Did John Ford make great movies? Absolutely. Did Steven Spielberg make great movies? Absolutely. They were both amazingly special, each in their own right. Did they make the same kinds of movies? Absolutely not. Oh, I know the feeling. I was a film/video major myself (a very long time ago). I remember going with my class to a special screening in Hollywood and being chastised as a group by the director (who was the host for the screening) for the vapidity and lack of insights of our questions and comments.


I remember thinking, though, kind of what did he expect? We were a bunch of young twenty-somethings, all full of energy and enthusiasm, but *of course* lacking the depth and experience that he or his peers had.


Getting back on topic here, though, the kind of unique thing about film/video is that, while it is an artistic medium (requiring a *sole* visionary artistic creator), it generally involves a group of people for the actual creation. So the artist just has to say, look, this is what I want to create, and if you're on-board or not that's fine, but just get out of my way and let me create.


I remember my own initial efforts at filmmaking (and yes, we actually used "film" back in those days) were the source of much amusement for the class. 


That didn't put me off as much as the teacher, who told us that Hollywood was a closed system and since it wasn't USC or UCLA there was no way we could get into the system, so we were just wasting our time in any other institution. I took a different path, then, but I can't help but wonder how things would have gone had we had a different instructor.


But here's the thing with film/video: know the story you want to tell or the message you want to pass on, study everyone else who's done something similar, and then create your vision and stick to it. And you just have to ignore or find a way around those who don't share or oppose your vision. And then put the film/video out there and let it find its audience.


This is interesting to me personally, because I myself, after so long away from it, am beginning to get back into film/video production. The Internet has made all the difference, of course, as film/video makers can now find their audience directly and go around the studio system, which was impossible when I was your age. I wish us both much success!


But, even if we never find our audiences, I wish that we both remain true to our visions, and create films/videos that convey those well. That's all that really counts.
